title: Leading for equity: Educational leadership at the intersection of bilingualism and special education in an urban elementary school
abstract: This article examines how educational leadership is mobilized in efforts to foster equity at the intersection of bilingualism and special education in a large urban U.S. elementary school. Although bilingual education and special education (SPED) have developed robust but largely separate traditions, their convergence remains under-theorized, often rendering emergent bilingual students with disabilities institutionally invisible. Using a critical, practitioner-led interpretive case study informed by transformative leadership and intersectionality, the study analyzes documents, school-based observations, and reflexive practitioner records. The analysis identifies four mutually reinforcing leadership practices: reframing bilingualism as an instructional and interpretive asset; disrupting deficit discourses in referral, IEP, and classroom talk; fostering cross-departmental collaboration between bilingual and SPED structures; and embedding family and community voices in decision-making. These practices are synthesized into an Equity Cycle Model that conceptualizes leadership as an iterative process of discursive, organizational, and relational mediation rather than a one-off interventi

title: Defending the university against bad-faith policy interventions: Equality, diversity and inclusion, free speech, and institutional power
abstract: Recently, there has been a resurgence of claims that equality, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) initiatives threaten freedom of speech in UK higher education. Using the Alumni for Free Speech (AFFS) report (2025) as an example of this, we argue that the opposition between free speech and EDI is a politically manufactured false binary that obscures how power, voice, and harm are unevenly distributed within universities. Drawing on Critical Race Theory, decolonial scholarship, Black Radical Politics, and critical policy analysis, we conceptualise free speech as a socially stratified and relational resource rather than a neutral, universally accessible right. We show how the AFFS report mobilises methodological weaknesses, selective metrics, and claims of neutrality to construct EDI as a risk, deflecting attention from structural inequalities produced by racialised capitalism. Against this framing, we advance the claim that equity is not antithetical to academic freedom but a necessary condition for it, enabling participation, belonging, and knowledge production for marginalised groups within the academy. title: Education as commodity: A critical discourse analysis of the marketisation of higher education in India
abstract: This paper employs Fairclough’s Critical Discourse Analysis to examine how neoliberal rationalities are discursively legitimised within Indian higher education policy. Drawing on Giroux’s critical pedagogy and Foucault’s governmentality framework – used here as an integrated rather than parallel analytic – the study analyses the National Education Policy 2020 and related instruments. The paper argues that Indian higher education marketisation operates through a distinctive mechanism wherein the state simultaneously invokes constitutional social justice commitments toward Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, and Economically Weaker Sections while embedding market structures that undermine those commitments. Textual analysis reveals specific discursive strategies: the substitution of ‘scholarships’ and ‘targeted opportunities’ for the constitutional language of ‘reservation’; the repackaging of market deregulation as ‘autonomy’; and the deployment of equity vocabulary as rhetorical legitimation alongside provisions advancing privatisation. The study extends Giroux’s critical pedagogy by demonstrating that his class-based framework requires supplementation with

title: Suffering through shuttering: Closure, identity, and subjectification at a Japanese women’s university
abstract: This study explores how institutional closure shapes the subjectivities and identity formation of current and former students at a small-scale Japanese women’s university. Drawing on an Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis of six participant interviews, we employ Foucauldian readings of governmentality, subjectification, and discourse to understand how closure operates as a form of institutional power. Findings reveal that closure policies produce ‘rational’ subjectivities, characterised by pragmatic individualism, affective disengagement, and entrepreneurial self-governance. More damagingly, however, the accounts of participants in this study suggest that neoliberal governance within this institutional context positioned students as ‘docile’ subjects who navigated institutional precarity primarily through processes of self-responsibilisation. Within this case, institutional closure emerges as a site where market rationalities were enacted, normalised, and internalised through self-management and adaptation. In doing so, our research contributes to understandings of educational policy as a technology of power that shapes not only institutional futures but also the identities an

title: Beyond generic induction: Supporting novice Bedouin Arab female teachers through the academic incubator model in Israel
abstract: This qualitative phenomenological study examines the induction experiences of novice Bedouin Arab female teachers in Israel through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Drawing on in-depth interviews, the findings indicate that entry into teaching extends beyond a professional transition, constituting a socio-cultural process shaped by intersecting gender norms, community expectations, and hierarchical school structures. Participants described navigating a “double burden” of developing pedagogical competence while adhering to culturally embedded expectations of modesty and respect for authority. School-based relationships, including principals, mentors, and colleagues, were found to both support and constrain the satisfaction of teachers’ basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. At the same time, the Academic Incubator model functioned as an alternative professional space that enabled emotional support, reflective learning, and the gradual reconstruction of professional identity. The study contributes to research on teacher induction by demonstrating how power relations, minority status, and gender intersect to shape early career experiences and

title: Family-school collaboration for students with learning disabilities: Parental perspectives on inclusive education
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of educational support for students with learning disabilities in elementary schools in the Arab community in Israel. Through interviews with ten parents, the research examines three key areas: Individualized Educational Programs (IEPs), family-school communication, and inclusive practices. Findings reveal that schools implement personalized approaches, including in-class assistance, additional teaching hours, and therapeutic interventions. While many parents express satisfaction, some call for more tailored IEPs. Communication between schools and families varies in quality and frequency, with some parents desiring more detailed feedback on their child’s challenges and learning. Inclusive practices and extracurricular involvement are generally positive, though inconsistent across schools. The study concludes that schools are making significant efforts to support students with learning abilities, but there is room for improvement in personalizing IEPs, enhancing communication, and ensuring consistent inclusion. Based on the results, the researcher recommends that schools refine IEPs, improve coordination among service providers, increase spe

title: From theory to practice: Developing and applying educational indicators for Just Transition pedagogy
abstract: This study develops and applies educational indicators for Just Transition pedagogy, addressing the lack of tools that connect education to struggles for both social justice and critical environmental concerns. Drawing on literature in Just Transition, critical pedagogy, and sustainability education, thirteen indicators were created across three constructs: critical thinking, coexistence, and student agency. These were applied to analyze two graduate-student lesson plans on Indigenous peoples and sustainable tourism in Taiwan. Strong intercoder reliability between human and AI-assisted coders confirmed the robustness of the indicators as tools for curriculum analysis. The analysis showed that the lesson plans encourage learners to think critically, foster coexistence, and strengthen agency in resisting injustice within the context of Just Transition. Yet, a central challenge persisted: local issues were insufficiently connected to global concerns. This underscores the need for education to link local and global struggles, making visible the importance of transnational solidarity as a cornerstone of Just Transition, while the theoretical framework developed here highlights the poten

title: Rewriting professionalism in early childhood education and care: A call to collective agency
abstract: Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) professionals in England operate within a system that persistently undermines their status, voice, and agency. This conceptual paper, informed by prior empirical research, introduces a new conceptual framework positioning professional confidence as a driver of change from within the sector. Building on Miller’s analysis of system conditions that constrain professional identity and autonomy (2019; 2021), it reframes confidence not as an individual trait but as a relational, collective force. The conceptual framework identifies five interconnected components – awareness, positive action, skilful advocacy, collective action, and purposeful passion – through which practitioners can exercise meritocratic agency and challenge externally imposed definitions of professionalism. By situating confidence within the broader system architecture, the paper highlights how professional self-definition and sector-led leadership can begin to reshape institutional cultures. It concludes with a call to action for leaders, policymakers, and practitioners to co-create an empowered and self-determining profession.

title: Pedagogy of avoidance: Teachers’ and students’ approaches to the Israel–Palestine conflict and manifestations of antisemitism in Swedish Schools
abstract: Recent reports from a number of Swedish municipalities show increased levels of antisemitism since the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. This underlines the challenges faced by schools in addressing antisemitism. Despite increasing reports of antisemitism in Swedish schools, little is known about how educators and students navigate these issues within multireligious school environments. This case study focuses on an urban secondary school in Sweden, which has Jewish students and topics on Jewish life and Judaism, and examines how issues related to antisemitism and the Israeli–Palestinian (I–P) conflict are addressed within a multireligious school environment. This qualitative study draws on interviews with six school leaders, two special pedagogues, five social studies teachers, and four student focus groups, with five students in each ( n = 33). The findings reveal that although some antisemitic incidents have occurred at the school, interviewees report that such events are relatively infrequent. Students perceive the school as safe, but conflicts and polarised positionings regarding the I–P conflict create an uneasy environment, especially for Jewish students, who are oft

title: Between flexibility and precarity: Part-time English teachers in Macau’s universities and their educational pathways
abstract: This paper examines part-time English teachers’ experiences in higher education in Macau, focusing on their motivations, challenges, and career pathways in an environment marked by flexibility and precarity. Through qualitative interviews with seven part-time instructors, the research investigates themes such as online teaching practice, the balance between the conflicting demands of teaching and research, and collegiality. The findings elucidate the dualities of part-time employment, where autonomy and flexible scheduling are paired with job insecurity, limited career advancement, and emotional strain. The study calls for institutional support, revised evaluation frameworks, and collaborative cultures to enhance the well-being and professional development of part-time instructors. Addressing these dynamics would enable higher education to productively utilize the knowledge of part-time educators towards enhancing educational quality and the regional development agenda.

title: “Communication between Bedouin kindergarten teachers and parents during war: WhatsApp’s key role”
abstract: The role of the kindergarten teacher is especially important in early childhood, particularly in conflict-affected regions where social and educational structures face unique challenges. This study examines the impact of war on communication between kindergarten teachers and parents in the Bedouin Arab sector in Israel, a minority community with distinct socio-economic and cultural characteristics. The research focuses on the wartime period, during which remote teaching became necessary, and explores the use of WhatsApp as the primary communication tool in compulsory and pre-compulsory kindergartens. A qualitative methodology was employed, involving 20 semi-structured interviews with Arab kindergarten teachers. The findings reveal that during the war, WhatsApp was preferred over other digital platforms due to infrastructural limitations in unrecognized Bedouin villages and the specific socio-economic challenges faced by the community, including a lack of access to stable internet and advanced digital devices among parents. WhatsApp was widely used for educational purposes, messaging, instructions, storytelling, and activities, proving to be more effective than Zoom, which teachers

title: Education, alienation and marginalisation: Neoliberalism and the politics of exclusion
abstract: This study draws on critical perspectives on power and politics to demonstrate how exclusion is structurally embedded within educational systems. Although, the claim that education produces marginalisation may initially appear rhetorical. While education is often presented as a tool for empowerment, knowledge production and social mobility, it can also marginalise communities by pushing them out through official knowledge structures and tokenistic inclusion. Using the critical theory of education, the study questions the dominant forms of knowledge that are designed in a way to serve the interests of elites and corporate actors. Often, the frameworks exclude tribal communities from policymaking, neglect their knowledge systems, and detach them from their sustainable ways of living. Drawing on ethnographic methods, this study engages closely with tribal community members in Ladakh (India) through long-term interaction and participation for 14 months. It reveals how education contributes to social exclusion and how market forces aligned with neoliberal agendas that shape the educational experiences of tribal communities.

title: Leadership agility and institutional resilience: The mediating roles of digital readiness and strategic adaptation in Chinese higher education digital transformation
abstract: As higher education institutions (HEIs) navigate complex digital transformation demands, leadership agility has emerged as a critical determinant of institutional resilience. This study examined the mechanisms through which leadership agility is associated with institutional resilience, focusing on the mediating roles of digital readiness and strategic adaptation, and the moderating role of organizational innovation climate. Data were collected from 445 senior administrators across Chinese HEIs, including vice chancellors, deans, directors, and heads of departments. Participants completed validated scales measuring leadership agility, digital readiness, strategic adaptation, innovation climate, and institutional resilience. Structural equation modeling was employed to test direct, mediated, and moderated pathways. Results revealed significant associations between leadership agility and institutional resilience (β = 0.28), digital readiness (β = 0.52), and strategic adaptation (β = 0.30). Mediation analyses indicated indirect statistical pathways linking leadership agility with institutional resilience (β = 0.09). Furthermore, organizational innovation climate significantly moderate

title: Educational critical theory: A path forward
abstract: This paper has three aims. First, to provide a critical history (to look back critically at the community you belong to) of the ECT (Educationalists that adopt a critical theory perspective) to see how the major contributors to this community developed their approach to critical theory with an educational emphasis and more specifically how they looked at the relation between economics (a Marxist approach) and culture. Second, with the major finding of this critical history being that Marxism and economics was deemphasized within this community (of which I am a member) and the cultural became the dominant orientation, the paper considers what limits this focus had and has on critiquing society to change it. The third aim is to consider an alternative to this cultural emphasis that is titled Oneness theory—the weaving together of culture and economics. The thesis of Oneness theory is that by weaving culture and economics together not only will injustices and possibilities be more fully understood but differing critical theory groups can work together in solidarity to become a force for change to a more just society.

title: Politics, economics, and identity: Mapping a virtual linguistics landscape in Indonesia
abstract: Jakarta’s Virtual Linguistic Landscape (VLL) offers a unique lens for examining the intersection of politics, economics, and identity in a multilingual, globalized urban setting. While most linguistic landscape studies focus on physical spaces, this research maps Jakarta’s VLL by analyzing language use in street, store, and restaurant names across five culturally and economically distinct districts: Glodok, Tanah Abang, Menteng, Thamrin-Sudirman, and Condet & Cipayung. Using virtual ethnography, data were collected from Google Maps, business directories, and online images, then analyzed through Thematic Analysis and Critical Discourse Analysis. Findings show that Bahasa Indonesia dominates official toponymy due to state policy, while commercial actors strategically deploy English for global prestige, Mandarin and Arabic for ethnocultural identity, and Betawi dialect for local preservation. District-level variations reveal how language functions as both a political instrument and an economic commodity. The study concludes that Jakarta’s VLL reflects broader socio-political power structures, market-driven language commodification, and community identity negotiation, underscoring the

title: Rethinking race theory in education: Racial Value Theory (RVT)
abstract: Race theory in education is locked into a mode of critique that accepts conventional categories of political economy and essentialises race and education as timeless. Attempts to build economic factors into CRT (Critical Race Theory) and recent attempts to combine CRT with theories of racialised social systems to create Racialised Social Systems (RSS) Theory do not enable a negative critique of capitalism. Social Reproduction Theory (SRT) and Marxist theories of racialisation do engage with a negative critique of capitalism but could further consider the contradictions of capitalist society. This requires an understanding of capitalism, class struggle and race that transcends naïve materialism and enables an understanding of education, race and capitalism as locked into permanent crisis. Using metatheoretical critique, a new metatheory, Racial Value Theory (RVT) is presented. This shows how methods of ‘racial organisation’, racial categorisations and racial theories in education become archaic. For educators, RVT shows the redundancy of forms of practice and praxis but also the possibilities for revolutionary education.

title: Higher education and the Western cannon of thoughts: Are Southern African universities bewitched?
abstract: Notwithstanding the frantic efforts by Southern African universities to decolonise education, evidence persists to show that their education systems are predominantly shaped by Western epistemologies, obscuring our understanding on whether these institutions are cursed by coloniality to perpetuate colonial legacies. Through a comprehensive literature review and theoretical analysis, the paper, anchored on the decolonial theory, explores whether the universities in Southern Africa are bewitched or otherwise, and then proposes pathways toward decolonisation and epistemic justice. The analysis reveals that the metaphor of ‘bewitchment’ aptly describes the entrapment of universities within the colonial structures, where alternative knowledge systems are marginalised and excluded. From the findings, the study recommends that universities commit to structural changes that include the indigenisation of universities in Africa, the integration of indigenous knowledge systems, the use of local languages and the development of curricula that reflect the socio-cultural realities of the region. Only through such comprehensive efforts can these institutions overcome the bewitchment of colonialit

title: Why cultural competency in higher education must Be tailored: Lessons from Britain and France
abstract: Cultural competency is widely recognised as essential in modern higher education, given the increasing prevalence of culturally diverse student bodies. However, turning that recognition into educational practices that align with the social and cultural realities of each country is challenging. This article argues that prevailing approaches to cultural competency often ignore the ideological frameworks in which they are embedded. Drawing on the contrasting cases of Britain and France, where celebratory multiculturalism and assimilationist republicanism, respectively, shape educational norms, we reveal how cultural engagement is too often constrained by national traditions. We advocate for a reconceptualisation of cultural competency as a dynamic, context-sensitive pedagogical practice rather than a universalised skillset. Grounded in the scholarship of critical pedagogy and intercultural learning, and speaking to an international audience of educators, this work calls for tailored, reflexive approaches that interrogate underlying assumptions and work towards genuinely inclusive and transformative educational experiences across diverse global settings.

title: Resisting and reproducing colonialism in Jamaican education: A scoping review of curriculum, pedagogy, and policy (1947–2025)
abstract: Jamaica’s education system continues to reflect the imprint of colonial rule, as Eurocentric curricula, rigid language hierarchies, and high-stakes testing reproduce inequities despite repeated reforms. Political independence did not dismantle these structures and attempts to democratize access have often been undermined by persistent stratification. At the same time, teachers and policymakers have experimented with reforms aimed at equity, inclusion, and cultural responsiveness. This scoping review synthesizes 45 studies published between 1947 and 2025 to examine how colonial and postcolonial dynamics have shaped Jamaican education across history, policy, and pedagogy. The analysis maps developments in curriculum, language policy, assessment, teacher education, and culturally responsive pedagogy (CRP). Findings demonstrate the endurance of colonial structures in school categorization, curricular content, and testing practices, while initiatives such as the National Standards Curriculum sought, with mixed results, to redress inequities. Teachers often resist systemic constraints through CRP, such as affirming Jamaican Creole and integrating local knowledge, though institutional sup

title: Neoliberal policy as racism in secondary education England and Germany: Whiteness as capital in racial capitalism
abstract: This paper provides an analysis of the relationship between neoliberal reform in secondary education in England and Germany and the reproduction of racial inequality. We fill a gap in the understanding of how neoliberal mechanisms interact with racial structures in secondary education to fuel race inequality. The paper reviews existing literature on neoliberal policies in secondary education. We employ insights from theories of racial capitalism (Gerrard et al., 2022) and innovatively combine these with an understanding of whiteness as symbolic racial capital (Reiter, 2020). The paper identifies common neoliberal mechanisms in secondary education in both countries: school choice, institutional autonomy, and responsibilisation of the individual. We demonstrate that neoliberal mechanisms function to create racialised divisions in both education systems by fuelling: • ethnic segregation, • the exclusion of minority groups from mainstream educational spaces, • and cultural ‘othering’. Our analysis shows that these divisions are achieved by the education systems enabling the extraction and realisation of value via the fuelling of the prestige and desirability of whiteness, and practices

title: Policy implementation, trust, and fear of the unknown in Greek schools: Barriers and opportunities for educational reform
abstract: Teacher evaluation and accountability have become central to educational reform in Greece since 2012, a system marked by strong centralization and political volatility. This study explores how Greek teachers interpret and respond to policy reforms that are often introduced without sufficient consultation or support, creating conditions of mistrust and fear of change. Drawing on thirteen semi-structured interviews with teachers, headteachers, and regional officials, the study adopts an interpretivist, policy enactment framework to examine how educators construct meaning around evaluation, trust, and professional autonomy. The thematic analysis identified four interrelated themes: top-down control and systemic dependence, mistrust and political influence, fear of the unknown, and professional autonomy as stability. Findings reveal that teachers’ resistance is not rooted in opposition to change but in defensive responses to instability and opaque policy communication. Trust emerged as a critical condition for reform engagement, underscoring the need for dialogue and sustained collaboration between policymakers and practitioners. The study contributes to international debates on educat

title: Cultural Diversity Awareness Scale (CDAS) for multi-ethnic students
abstract: Various studies have been conducted to develop instruments for measuring cultural diversity awareness, but there are still very few or not specific to multi-ethnic students in North Maluku. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to develop and validate the Cultural Diversity Awareness Scale (CDAS) from the perspective of multi-ethnic students in secondary schools, through four stages: defining and compiling constructs, conducting first trials, conducting analysis, revising instruments, and checking instrument validity. The sample of this study was 300 multi-ethnic students in senior high schools spread across seven districts/cities in North Maluku province, Indonesia, using a multistage cluster sampling technique. The results of the construct validity study revealed three main indicators, 11 sub-indicators, 17 descriptors, and 57 items. Then, the results of the content validity test on the 57 items eliminated seven, leaving 50 remaining. Statistical tests using product-moment on the 50 CDAS statement items showed that 39 items were valid, while 11 items were invalid. title: Hybrid governmentality: A Foucauldian analysis of power-knowledge dynamics in Ethiopian education system (1991–2018)
abstract: This study provides a Foucauldian genealogical analysis of the power and knowledge dynamics that shaped Ethiopia’s education system from 1991 to 2018. The analysis explores how a new governmental rationality, a hybrid of the ruling party’s “revolutionary democracy” and a global neoliberal discourse, was produced and institutionalized. Using policy documents and secondary sources, the study reveals four key findings: first, the state used disciplinary technologies to co-opt educational institutions and produce politically compliant subjects. Second, donor-driven reforms acted as a powerful form of governmentality, establishing a neoliberal regime of truth that prioritized market efficiency over academic expertise. Third, the resulting tension between quantity and quality was a predictable outcome of a biopolitical project that normalized mediocrity in favor of mass enrollment. Finally, these dynamics led to the systemic epistemic suppression and knowledge dispossession of Ethiopian academics. The study concludes that during this period, education was not a neutral social good but a central site for the exercise of power, where global and local forces converged to shape knowledge, pr

title: Changes in Hong Kong’s education policies and conditions in recent years under the atmosphere of Chinese-style political correctness
abstract: Since the 2019 Anti-Extradition Law Amendment Bill Movement, both the Chinese government and the Hong Kong government, along with pro-establishment figures, have attributed the political unrest to perceived problems within Hong Kong’s education system. In response, the Hong Kong government has increasingly aligned itself with Chinese-style political correctness. This study adopts “Chinese-style political correctness” as an analytical lens to investigate recent changes in Hong Kong’s educational policies and conditions. It first reviews developments in education policy from the 1997 handover to the 2019 movement, and then applies discourse analysis to official documents to examine how these texts reflect shifts in education policy after 2019. Supplementary sources are used to contextualize these changes within broader societal developments. The findings suggest that, under the prevailing discourse of political correctness, education policies have tilted toward values endorsed by the Chinese government, such as patriotism, national education, and nationalism. These trends have contributed to structural and cultural transformations in the educational landscape, including the dissoluti

title: Renegotiating the relationship between HBCUs and state higher education boards to address coloniality
abstract: State higher education coordinating and governing boards play a tremendous role in the oversight, regulation, and success of institutions. State funding policies significantly impact the survival and growth of Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). The relationship between HBCUs and state governments has historically not been harmonious, largely due to systemic white hegemony, which perpetuated legalized and subversive racial segregation and oppression. This long history of racism has manifested in many ways, including strategically designed policies meant to create inequities in resource allocation and oversight for HBCUs. In this conceptual paper, we identify how HBCUs and their advocates interact with state higher education coordinating and governing boards to engage in policymaking to support HBCUs and their students, as well as underlying political-historical and socio-cultural triggers that inform this relationship. This analysis highlights problems with white colonial perspectives and approaches to state policymaking for HBCUs. We conclude by pointing out gaps and opportunities for both research and practice on the relationship between state higher education c

title: Decolonising postgraduate supervision: Rebalancing power dynamics in African university contexts
abstract: Postgraduate supervision in African universities continues to be influenced by colonial legacies that favour hierarchical, expert-dominated approaches to knowledge production. This study proposes a decolonial reimagining of supervision through a theoretically grounded and practically relevant framework that centres on power redistribution, cultural affirmation, and mutual knowledge construction. Drawing on critical decolonial theory and African indigenous knowledge systems, the research employs a theory synthesis design and conceptual analysis to interrogate dominant supervisory norms and reconstruct them within a relational and context-responsive paradigm. Three interdependent dimensions – relational reciprocity, cultural relevance, and dialogic reflexivity – emerge as the foundational pillars of a heuristic model for decolonial supervision. This model situates the supervisory relationship as a site of shared scholarly agency, where both supervisor and candidate co-construct research grounded in ethical engagement, indigenous epistemologies, and reflexive practice. The framework not only contributes conceptually to the literature on postgraduate education but also provides actiona

title: Narratives of teachers’ experiences of structural violence in farm schools in Mpumalanga, South Africa
abstract: Structural violence is often overlooked when exploring school violence and its consequences for teaching and learning. However, it is the deadliest form of violence that breeds direct and cultural violence. It accounts for inequalities in access to educational opportunities, healthcare, and poverty. Against this backdrop, this study explores teachers’ experiences of structural violence in farm schools. Situated within the interpretivism paradigm, I employed narrative inquiry as a research methodology to inquire about teachers’ lived experiences of structural violence within the farm school context. Four teachers were purposively selected to participate in this study. I employed focus group interviews as an instrument of generating data; focus group interviews allowed participants to collectively narrate their experiences of structural violence during their teaching career. The study reveals that teachers and learners in farm schools are victims of structural violence observed through dilapidated school infrastructure, asbestos roofings, overcrowding, and high levels of learner dropout. Due to the low enrolment rate, teachers are overloaded with work, resulting in fatigue and emotio

title: Potential of schools to promote spatial solidarity by recognising intergenerational power relations: Staff perspective
abstract: The paper is based on a study where 24 staff members of a school in Finland were asked to complete fictional post-apocalypse stories in an investigation interested in the rationales underlying sources of solidarity in school. The research was motivated by the idea that intergenerational solidarity is vital to young people’s wellbeing because it can promote young people’s participation in schools. Drawing on the concept of spatial solidarity, the analysis reveals three sources of solidarity: interdependency, norms and values, and intergenerational conflict. The findings highlight that solidarities in school derive from place-based power dynamics that can sustain adult centric hierarchies but also have the potential to lead to genuine intergenerational collaboration. Understanding these sources of solidarity can help adults working with young people to critically reflect on how they contribute to the world beyond the individual and how a democratic outlook on power relations can be realized in intergenerational communities.

title: 21st century student government at the international level: Eurocentrism and isolationism
abstract: Student government at the international level has great potential to improve the quality of education of students around the world. However, in the first quarter of the twenty-first century, it has been hindered by Eurocentrism while much of the world’s students outside of Europe face substantial barriers to participation. I present an autoethnographic analysis drawing from my experience as an elected student representative in multiple international student governments to explore the ways in which the systemic barriers facing student representation beyond campus and national borders manifest and these barriers' impacts on the world’s students. I provide recommendations for ways international student government can improve its capabilities and become more representative and equitable.

title: Retraction: Interpersonal communication as an acmeological problem in contemporary education
Investigating the value of crisis management in a Greek school environment using experimental and econometrical analysis
abstract: Teachers’ perceptions in dealing effectively with critical situations are particularly critical as they can prepare both their students and the school environment to improve the way they recognize and manage school crises and unexpected situations that may occur in their everyday lives. This study investigated, through econometric and experimental analysis, the sampled Greek teachers’ actual behavior and perceptions regarding the existence of crises in the school environment and how they should be managed. The results revealed that students’ misbehavior is the primary problem in schools while parental collaboration with the school and the formation of the crisis management teams can make crisis management more effective. The study’s contribution to the literature, through the experimental and econometrical analysis of attitudes toward crisis management in schools, is twofold: (a) to reveal teachers’ perceived priorities in various crises, which otherwise would not have happened, and (b) to extend the link between organizational theory and crisis management in schools. This study suggests that the importance of crisis management in schools is increasing due to its significant contri

title: Do residential colleges promote sustainable education and reduce educational disparities based on gender and socioeconomic background?
abstract: As the cornerstone of the fourth Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) that was developed by the United Nations, equitable access to high-quality education is universally acknowledged as a fundamental human right and a major force that makes economic progress possible. This objective is nevertheless hampered by enduring gender and socioeconomic status (SES) disparities that are maintained by the current power structure and workings of society. In public institutions, the use of residential colleges (RCs) is a strategy that has produced favourable outcomes. On the other hand, the usefulness of RCSs in Chinese private universities has received less attention. Evaluating RCSs’ contribution to sustainable development in public and private higher education is the goal of this article. RC students and non-RC students – two categories of university students – were surveyed. The analysis, which employs a quantitative research methodology, demonstrates that RC is not always effective in guaranteeing children from all socioeconomic backgrounds for an equitable opportunity to education. The difference in admissions is noticeable in private colleges especially. However, in both public and pri

title: Racial discourse as praxis: Reflections on becoming an anti-racist through a university-level course power and education
abstract: This qualitative study captures the narrative of six culturally diverse doctoral students’ after they have participated in an anti-racist course. The course immersed students in literature surrounding race and school-based criminalization to heighten their awareness of ways internalized racism and perpetuated anti-Black racism harms the students they educate. Within this study, we conducted two focus group sessions and analyzed responses from six doctoral students at Wayne State University. As they reflected on the racism being perpetuated in education and their daily challenges within a system based on white supremacy, they ignited their determination to work for racial equity having realized their past contributions to perpetuating these ideologies. Critical race theory (CRT) was used to take a deeper look at the historical and ongoing aspect of race and racism in American culture, including within the education system. The participants of color discussed their personal experiences with oppression as well as their initial resistance to become anti-racist. At the end of the course, that resistance evolved into an increased desire for racial advocacy. This study implicates that tea

title: Emancipatory Education and the Challenge of Indoctrination: The Case of Internal Critique
abstract: This theoretical article examines whether critical political education—understood as education that critiques society from within—can avoid the challenge of indoctrination. To this end, the article reconstructs the premises of critical political education, the concept of internal critique, Michael Walzer’s theory of internal critique, Hermann Giesecke’s conflict analysis model, and key criteria for identifying indoctrination in political education. It then develops a model of internal critique for political education and evaluates whether this model constitutes indoctrination. The conclusion offers a theoretical account of the indoctrination challenge in political education that operates through internal critique. The study argues that internal critique can function either as indoctrination or as a safeguard against it, depending on how effectively teachers implement the didactic principles of self-reflectivity, controversy, and dialogic teaching. When applied successfully, these principles allow the challenge to be avoided.

title: Educational leadership for social transformation - IEAL-J: Readiness, resilience, Re-imagination
Gender perspective in teacher education curriculum as an instrument of patriarchy’s persistence
abstract: This study aims to explore the gender perspective that interacts with the elementary school teacher education curriculum. Elementary school teachers are important in providing a foundation for elementary school students. So, we use that reason to conduct this study: the teachers’ perspective is obtained when they take teacher education studies. Ethnographic methods are used to observe the distribution of gender discourse in the elementary school teacher education curriculum for one semester. Elementary school teacher education students gain knowledge and exchange ideas in the classroom, and they also exchange ideas outside the classroom. The curriculum as a reflection of culture is obvious in this situation. However, the absence of planning regarding gender discourse so that it can be included in the curriculum makes patriarchy flow freely in it. title: The ambiguities of autonomy in youth training programmes
abstract: In recent decades, young people have been provided with various support systems, including therapeutic training programmes to enhance their mental health and well-being through empowerment and support of individual autonomy. In this paper, we examine the ideal of autonomy professed by training programmes for young people. We focused on analysing the inherent ambivalence surrounding the nature of this autonomy, and its manifestation in two youth support systems, specifically cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) based training programmes. By utilising Michel Foucault’s theoretical work on ‘technologies of the self’, we examined how these training programmes aim to guide individuals to transform themselves, and how they define the boundaries of autonomy within practice. Our findings indicate that rather than a stable capacity, autonomy emerges as a dynamic ideal that is always on the verge of its opposite – heteronomy. These programmes not only assume autonomy but require its ongoing cultivation through structured psychological labour. title: Superintendent leadership for teacher retention: Combating burnout in teachers of color and fostering well-being through a social justice lens
abstract: This conceptual synthesis paper examines the essential role of educational leaders in reducing teacher burnout and promoting well-being through a social justice framework. By exploring systemic challenges, culturally responsive practices, and the unique experiences of African American teachers, the paper highlights strategies for creating supportive and inclusive educational settings. This work addresses a gap in literature by proposing that teacher well-being and resilience should be integral professional responsibilities, emphasizing a humanizing and holistic view of educator sustainability. title: Behind the empty desks: Teachers’ insights into student absenteeism in India
abstract: This study explores teachers’ perspectives on student absenteeism in India’s elementary schools, with the goal of informing interventions and policies to tackle the issue of empty desks. It examines insights from 10 elementary teachers, gathered through in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and observations. The findings highlight a concerning trend in students' school absenteeism, revealing alarmingly low daily attendance rates of just 25–30% in many state government–run schools, particularly in rural areas. In stark contrast, private and central government schools enjoy significantly higher student attendance rates. Despite government initiatives addressing historical socio-economic factors like poverty, communication, or distance, absenteeism persists primarily due to stakeholders’ attitudinal integrity issues and a ‘poverty of minds’, including parental indifference, student demotivation, and falsified school reports. Teachers identified significant academic and behavioural impacts on students, alongside challenges in maintaining continuity and morale in classrooms. title: The impact of global-intercultural competence and social capital on students’ motivation to participate in exchange programs: A PLS-SEM approach
abstract: The current study investigated the correlation between cross-cultural competence, global competence, social capital, and their incidence in exchange motivation of students in the framework of national and international exchange programs. The study used a modified tool from a recognized framework. G*Power was used to select 303 students from 501 total population from Indonesia and the Philippines. A higher-order causal model was proposed following the partial least squares (PLS) method of structural equation models. The latent factor, global competence, was a higher-order factor containing the lower-order factors of global knowledge, global skills, and global skills. The main result was that cross-cultural competence, global competence, and social capital explained 70.10% of students’ exchange motivation variance. Specifically, we found a substantial link between global competence, social capital, and student motivation. Personal values also affected cross-cultural competence, emphasizing the value of culture in exchange programs. title: Socioeconomic status and rural–urban inequalities in AI access and academic performance for engineering students from the TVET
abstract: This study investigates socioeconomic and rural–urban disparities in access to artificial intelligence (AI) among engineering students enrolled following the TVET path in Bangladesh. We further analyse how socioeconomic status (SES) and geographic location affect access to AI tools and their impact on academic performance. Using primary survey data from diploma engineering students, the study applies a probit model to evaluate AI access and a multivariable linear regression model to assess the influence of AI usage on academic outcomes. Results demonstrate that students from higher-SES backgrounds and especially those who come from urban backgrounds achieve academic performance levels 20% higher, likely due to increased access to technology and a more supportive educational environment. Conversely, students from lower-income and rural backgrounds experience restricted access and lower academic achievement. These findings underscore the necessity for targeted policy interventions, including subsidized access and improved rural digital infrastructure, to foster inclusive educational outcomes.
